1.pericope_label: David’s message of condolence to Hanun, and the outrage done to his messengers

schools.summary: Ellicott discounts the opening formula, which stands also at the head of the previous chapter and has no chronological significance, so that it fixes nothing about when these events fell; what it introduces is a fuller treatment of matter already glanced at, the conflict with Ammon now described at length and the overthrow of Hadadezer related a second time with additional details. He then collates the two accounts clause by clause, and his verdict varies. The name of Nahash Samuel omits while adding Hanun, and he judges the omissions in each perhaps accidental; the title sons of Ammon he takes to call attention to their tribal organisation; and the remainder of that verse he thinks made more perspicuous here than in Samuel by slight changes and additions. At the next verse, however, he will not give the chronicler the credit: the question whether David’s servants have not come to search and overthrow and spy out the land is hardly an improvement on Samuel, who has the princes speak of searching the city, meaning the capital, and he reports the versions divided, the Syriac and Arabic agreeing with Samuel in reading city while the Greek and Latin read land. Of the outrage he notes that Samuel specifies the shaving of half the beards, that where the garments were cut the chronicler has substituted a more decorous term than the one in Samuel, rendering it literally unto the extremities, and that the cutting was meant to make the men look like captives.

Clarke sets out the chapter as an argument, running from the congratulatory message to Hanun and the incivility shown the messengers, through David’s condoling with them and the hiring of two and thirty thousand chariots and the siege of Medeba, to Joab’s defeat of the Syrians and Ammonites, the killing of Shophach their general with seven thousand charioteers and forty thousand infantry, and the Syrians’ abandoning of the Ammonites to make peace. On the insult itself he restores precisely what Ellicott says the chronicler softened, giving the plain sense in Latin and citing the Targum and Jarchi and others for it, that the men were left exposed in what nature and decency require to be concealed.

Henry leaves the collation alone and reads the opening for its duties. It becomes good people to be neighbourly and especially to be grateful: David will pay respect to Hanun because he is his neighbour, and religion teaches us to be civil and obliging to all, to honour all men and to be ready to do all offices of kindness to those we live among, nor must difference in religion be any obstruction to this. Beyond neighbourliness there was a debt, since David remembered the kindness Hanun’s father had shown him; and those who have received kindness must return it as they have ability and opportunity, returning it to the children when those who showed it are gone. For what followed he reaches for the proverb of the ancients, that wickedness proceeds from the wicked.

debates.question: Does the chronicler improve on Samuel’s wording here?

positions.view: At the second verse yes, made more perspicuous by slight changes and additions; at the third hardly an improvement, and the versions divide over city or land

debates.question: What exactly was done to the messengers?

positions.view: Half the beards shaved, the garments cut to make them look like captives; the chronicler uses a more decorous term than Samuel
The plain and indecent sense, on the authority of the Targum and Jarchi: they were left exposed

outliers.claim: Alone in restoring the indelicate sense of the mutilation that the chronicler had softened and Ellicott had noted as softened.
Alone in reading the embassy as a lesson in neighbourliness and in the duty of returning kindness to the children of those who showed it.

themes: Now it came to pass after this, that Nahash the king of the children of Ammon died, and his son reigned in his stead
I will shew kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash, because his father shewed kindness to me
Are not his servants come unto thee for to search, and to overthrow, and to spy out the land?

6.pericope_label: The hired Syrian coalition, Joab caught between two fronts, and the rout of the allies

schools.summary: Ellicott argues that from this point the chronicler leaves his predecessor behind: up to here the narrative has substantially coincided with the account in Samuel and might have been derived immediately from it, but this verse and those following differ considerably from the older account and add one or two material facts, which suggest another source. He finds a mark of lateness in the wording, the verb for making themselves odious appearing in a unique Aramaized form of the same verb Samuel uses, which he glosses as having become in bad odour; and on the price paid he notes that the talent was a weight and not a coin, coined money being unknown at that epoch, reckoning the thousand talents of silver at some four hundred thousand pounds. On the muster he holds the two accounts in substantial accord, allowing that the source the chronicler followed did not state the relative strength of the contingents but observing that the totals answer each other, and he cautions that the expression thirty-two thousand chariotry is not to be pressed, the writer wishing to stress chariots and cavalry as the chief arm of the Aramaean states while being as concise as possible. The battle he describes as a problem of two fronts, rendering the clause literally as the front of the battle had become towards Joab, front and rear: the Ammonites lay before the city while their Aramaean allies stood at some distance in the plain, so that to attack either with his whole army would have left Joab exposed to the other. He identifies the city as Medeba, notes that Samuel repeats the names of the allied kings where this account does not, and reads Joab’s exhortation for its Hebrew, the same verb underlying both halves and the second in reflexive form, so that the whole runs be strong, and let us shew ourselves strong, while the committal to God runs in the Hebrew order, and Jehovah, the good in his own eyes may he do.

Clarke totals the older account and finds a mismatch: twenty thousand Syrians of Beth-rehob and Zoba, a thousand of Maacah and twelve thousand of Ish-tob, thirty-three thousand in all, with no mention there of chariots or cavalry; and he concludes that these cannot have been the whole army. A second difference he meets by chronology rather than arithmetic, observing that the chariots and horsemen out of Mesopotamia are not mentioned in the parallel place and probably did not arrive until the Ammonites and their other allies had already been defeated in the first battle. Wesley glosses the disputed term as Ellicott does, of thirty-two thousand men who fought partly from chariots and partly on foot with them or attending upon them, as the ancient manner of fighting was.

Henry draws the lesson from the Ammonites, that the hearts of sinners marked for ruin are hardened to their destruction. Seeing they had made themselves odious to David it would have been their wisdom to desire conditions of peace and to offer satisfaction for the injury they had done him, the rather because they had made themselves obnoxious not only to David but to the justice of God, who is King of nations and will assert the injured rights and maintain the violated laws of nations; but instead of this they prepared for war, and so brought the ruin upon themselves.

debates.question: Do the numbers of the allied host agree with Samuel?

positions.view: No: Samuel totals thirty-three thousand and mentions no chariots at all, and these cannot have been the whole army
Yes, in substantial accord; and "thirty-two thousand chariotry" is not to be pressed
The term covers men who fought from chariots or on foot alongside them

debates.question: Why does this account differ from Samuel from here on?

positions.view: It follows another source: the differences are considerable and add material facts
The Mesopotamian contingent simply arrived later, after the first battle

outliers.claim: Alone in arguing from the divergences that the chronicler followed a source independent of Samuel, and alone in explaining the tactical difficulty of Joab’s two fronts.
Alone in harmonising the Mesopotamian chariots by supposing they arrived only after the first battle was lost.

16.pericope_label: Hadarezer’s reinforcements from beyond the river, Shophach slain, and the Syrians’ submission

schools.summary: Ellicott uses the second muster to fix which campaign this is: where Samuel has Hadarezer send and draw forth his forces, this account has the Syrians send messengers, and the form of the name is important as helping to identify this campaign with the one described earlier in the book. Of the river he gives the Euphrates its names in turn as the Babylonians and Assyrians, the Arabs and the ancient Persians called it, deriving the whole from an Accadian compound meaning great river. One place-name he thinks the chronicler has quietly removed: Samuel says the armies came to Helam, where this account says only that David came upon them, and an intelligible phrase appears to have been substituted for the name of an unknown locality — the Hebrew for to Helam carrying the same consonants as the prepositional phrase standing here with one letter over, so that the substitution was easily made. He reports a suggestion made to him privately by Professor Sayce, that this mysterious Helam is no other than Aleppo, the Halman of the Assyrian monuments. On the casualty figures he declines to adjudicate: this account gives seven thousand chariotry and forty thousand footmen where Samuel reads seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen, and such deviations seem to indicate independent sources, so that we can hardly choose between the two accounts, though horsemen may be the more correct reading. The killing of Shophach he takes for an abridged statement of what Samuel gives more fully. The closing verse yields his sharpest observation, drawn from a single word: where this account has the tributaries make peace with David and become his servants, Samuel has them make peace with Israel and serve them, so that to the writer of Samuel God’s people is the main topic while to the chronicler it is the divinely anointed king — a difference slight in itself but characteristic of each.

Wesley turns the submission of the Syrians into counsel for the reader: let those who have in vain stood it out against God be thus wise for themselves, and let them become his servants, for they are undone if they remain his enemies.

debates.question: Can the two accounts of the casualties be reconciled?

positions.view: They indicate independent sources and we can hardly choose, though "horsemen" may be the more correct reading

debates.question: What became of Samuel’s place-name Helam?

positions.view: The chronicler substituted an intelligible phrase for an unknown locality; Sayce suggests Helam is Aleppo

outliers.claim: Alone in drawing a characteristic difference of interest between the two historians from the single change of "with Israel" to "with David", and alone in reporting Sayce’s private identification of Helam with Aleppo.
